introduction.title: Circuit function and components
definitions: Real devices are replaced by ideal elements and their connections for the calculation you need.
Converts another form of energy to electrical energy, or provides a signal.
Receives energy and converts it to light, heat, motion or another useful output.
Wires, switches, contacts, control and protective devices connect the parts.
Main purpose: generate, transmit or convert energy. Example: battery and lamp.
Main purpose: transmit or process information. Example: microphone → amplifier → loudspeaker, or temperature measurement.
In this course’s introductory terminology: contains a source / contains no source. A two-terminal network connects through two terminals.
The introductory DC model is constant. AC reverses direction or polarity; sinusoidal AC follows a sine wave.
rules: Closed conducting path → sustained current
Opening the path stops the steady current in the simple battery–switch–lamp circuit.
More load = more power consumption
At fixed supply voltage, greater power demand requires greater current; it does not mean greater resistance.
examples: Torch: battery = source; bulb = load; switch and contacts = intermediate link.
traps: The load converts energy; it does not consume the circulating charge.
A signal circuit still requires energy. Classify its principal purpose.

basics.title: Current, potential, voltage, power and energy
definitions: Charge crossing a section each second, not the speed of an individual electron. Conventional direction follows positive-charge motion.
Potential uses a chosen zero node. Voltage compares two specified points in a specified order.
Power is energy per second. Energy also depends on how long the transfer lasts.
rules: I = Q/t; i = dq/dt
Q/t is steady current, or average current over the interval. dq/dt gives instantaneous current.
Uab = Va − Vb
Use node potentials measured against the same reference.
P = UI
Positive absorbed power uses current entering the marked positive terminal.
W = Pt = UIt
Use constant power, voltage and current over the stated interval. Use seconds and amperes for joules.
kW measures power; kWh measures energy.
symbols: Time in seconds; charge’s rate of change, C/s.
Ordered voltage difference; node potentials, all in volts (V = J/C).
Energy, joules (J). Here W is a quantity symbol; W after a number is the watt unit.
examples: 6 C in 3 s → I = 2 A. A 6 V bulb taking 1.6 A absorbs 9.6 W.
2 V × 10 mA × 30 min: convert to 0.010 A and 1800 s → 36 J.
Teacher’s 10 V / two 2 Ω circuit: I = 2.5 A. With c = 0: Va = 10 V, Vb = 5 V. With a = 0: Va = 0, Vb = −5 V, Vc = −10 V. Uab stays 5 V.
traps: Changing ground shifts potentials, not physical voltage differences.
Convert mA to A and minutes to seconds before calculating energy.

emf.title: EMF and terminal voltage
definitions: Energy supplied per coulomb by the source’s non-electric energy-conversion process. It is measured in volts, not newtons.
Through the ideal source from − toward +: source action raises energy per positive charge.
The potential difference measured across the source’s actual output terminals.
Models internal voltage drop and heating while the source delivers current.
rules: U = Us − IR₀
For the practical source while current leaves its positive output terminal.
I = 0 → U = Us
Open output: no current-dependent internal drop.
R₀ = 0 → U = Us
An ideal voltage source keeps its prescribed voltage while delivering current too.
symbols: Internal resistance, ohms (Ω); 0 labels the internal part.
examples: 12 V EMF, internal 2 Ω and load 4 Ω → I = 2 A; internal drop = 4 V; output = 8 V.
Energy account per coulomb: 12 J supplied = 4 J internal heat + 8 J delivered outside.
traps: EMF, terminal voltage and node potential share a unit but describe different ideas.
Conventional external current runs from the positive output through the load toward the negative output. Do not confuse this with the EMF arrow.
The subtraction relation assumes delivery. Current pushed into the positive terminal changes the signed relation.

conditions.title: Loaded, open and shorted sources
definitions: A finite load completes the output path.
The external path is broken: branch current is zero; voltage may remain.
Output terminals are directly joined: their voltage difference is zero; current may remain.
rules: I = Us/(R₀ + R); U = IR = Us − IR₀
Loaded source; keep the internal and external resistances distinct.
I = 0; Uoc = Us; Pload = 0
Open output of this source model.
Isc = Us/R₀; U = 0
Shorted output, assuming nonzero internal resistance.
Psource = UsI; Pload = UI; Ploss = I²R₀
Source conversion = delivered load power + internal heat.
R₀ = (Us − U)/I
Infer internal resistance from loaded measurements with nonzero current.
symbols: EMF; terminal voltage; open-circuit terminal voltage, all volts (V).
Internal resistance; external load resistance, ohms (Ω).
Source conversion, delivered power and internal heat, watts (W).
examples: Teacher: Us = 125 V, U = 115 V, I = 4 A → R₀ = 2.5 Ω; 500 W supplied = 460 W delivered + 40 W internal heat.
12 V, R₀ = 2 Ω: an open gives 0 A and 12 V. A short gives 6 A and 0 V, with 72 W of internal heat.
traps: Zero terminal power during a short does not mean zero internal heating.
An ideal nonzero voltage source with zero internal resistance across an ideal short has no finite-current solution.
The teacher’s 125 V / 115 V example describes a loaded source, despite the reused shorting-line drawing.

signs.title: References and signed answers
definitions: The node assigned zero potential. It need not be physical earth.
An assigned arrow; a negative calculated current flows opposite that arrow.
Ordered subscripts or +/− marks identify the difference being calculated. The course voltage arrow runs from referenced + to referenced −.
rules: Uab = Va − Vb; Uba = −Uab
Keep the node identities fixed when reversing the voltage reference.
U = RI
Resistor current reference enters its marked positive terminal.
U = −RI
Current reference is reversed while the voltage reference is retained.
symbols: Potentials and ordered voltage differences, volts (V).
examples: Teacher: 10 V with 4 Ω + 3 Ω + 3 Ω → I = 1 A. With bottom d grounded: Va = 10 V, Vb = 6 V, Vc = 3 V.
Teacher midpoint between +12 V and −10 V through equal resistors: Vmid = −10 + (12 − (−10))/2 = 1 V.
traps: Choose references before calculating. Do not silently flip an arrow halfway through.
A negative result changes the interpretation relative to your reference, not the physical node labels.

sources.title: Ideal sources and supplied/absorbed power
definitions: Fixes its prescribed voltage; the connected circuit determines its current.
Fixes its prescribed current; the connected circuit determines its voltage.
Use the actual signed voltage/current references. A device named “source” can absorb energy.
rules: Pabs = UI
Current reference enters the marked + terminal. Positive means absorption; negative means supply.
Psupplied = −Pabs
The same transfer described as power supplied rather than absorbed.
symbols: Signed voltage in volts and current in amperes.
examples: 10 V source: one 2 Ω load takes 5 A; two such loads in parallel take 10 A total. Voltage stays 10 V.
1 A current source: output is 1 V across 1 Ω, and 10 V across 10 Ω. Current stays 1 A.
Teacher table below: upward 3 A current source and 3 V voltage source with + at the top. Negative absorption means delivery.
traps: The word “source” does not determine its power sign.
Check that total supplied power equals total absorbed power.

capacitor.title: Capacitor law
definitions: Charge stored per unit voltage. Equal and opposite charge builds on the two plates.
Capacitor current depends on the rate of voltage change, not voltage alone.
rules: q = Cu; i = dq/dt = C du/dt
Ideal constant capacitor, using passive references: current enters the marked positive terminal.
symbols: Capacitance, farads (F); do not confuse the symbol with the coulomb unit.
Voltage’s rate of change, volts per second (V/s).
examples: If voltage is constant in time, du/dt = 0, so the ideal capacitor current is zero.
traps: A capacitor may have nonzero voltage with zero steady current. Do not use i = u/R for its ideal element law.

inductor.title: Inductor law and opposing EMF
definitions: Relates voltage to the rate of change of current.
The induced EMF opposes the change in current; it does not simply oppose all current.
rules: uL = L diL/dt
Ideal constant inductor with current entering the marked positive voltage terminal.
e = −L diL/dt; uL = −e
The source’s induced-EMF reference is opposite to the passive terminal-voltage reference.
symbols: Terminal voltage and induced EMF, volts (V).
Current’s rate of change, amperes per second (A/s).
examples: Constant ideal-inductor current → diL/dt = 0 → terminal voltage is zero.
traps: Do not attach a minus sign to the passive voltage law without checking the references.
An actual coil’s wire resistance is separate from its ideal inductance.

transformation.title: Practical sources and source transformation
definitions: Ideal voltage source with series resistance.
Ideal current source with parallel resistance.
The same voltage–current relationship at the same two output terminals; internal power/currents can differ.
rules: U = Us − IR; Iout = Is − U/R
Output relations for supplying practical voltage/current sources.
Is = Us/R; Us = IsR
Finite nonzero R. Keep its value; series becomes parallel or vice versa.
I₁ = I R₂/(R₁ + R₂); I₂ = I R₁/(R₁ + R₂)
Two parallel resistors carrying total current I.
symbols: Ideal source voltage and output voltage, volts (V).
Ideal current source value, output current and total current, amperes (A).
examples: 10 V + series 2 Ω ↔ 5 A || 2 Ω. With a 3 Ω load, IL = 2 A either way.
Main course example: 5 V + 2 kΩ → 2.5 mA || 2 kΩ. Add the 2 mA source; combine shunts to 2/3 kΩ; external branch is 3 kΩ. IL = 9/11 mA ≈ 0.818 mA downward.
Final review: 40 V + 2 Ω and 20 V + 2 Ω parallel branches → 30 A || 1 Ω. With 4 Ω load: IL = 6 A and U = 24 V.
traps: Current-source arrow points toward the voltage source’s positive output terminal.
Do not transform an isolated ideal source into a finite opposite-type equivalent.
A resistor parallel to an ideal voltage source, or series with an ideal current source, can be omitted for some external calculations—not for its internal power.

topology.title: Nodes, branches, loops and meshes
definitions: The teacher’s junction where three or more elements meet. A connected unbroken conductor is one node.
Current path between essential nodes; it may contain multiple series elements.
A planar loop with no smaller loop inside it. A suitable set gives independent loop equations.
rules: Independent KCL equations = n − 1
For a connected circuit graph, using consistent node/branch definitions.
Independent loop equations = b − n + 1
Do not count every possible closed path as a new independent equation.
symbols: Number of nodes in the chosen graph.
Number of branches in the same graph.
examples: Teacher’s five-branch example: n = 3, b = 5 → two independent KCL and three independent loop equations.
traps: Some videos count ordinary two-element junctions as nodes. Follow your teacher’s essential-node/branch convention in the counting questions.

kirchhoff.title: KCL and KVL
definitions: Currents crossing a node or closed boundary balance. Internal currents cancel for a boundary around multiple components.
Signed voltage changes around a closed path sum to zero.
Moving from − to + is a voltage rise; moving from + to − is a voltage drop.
rules: ΣIenter = ΣIleave; Σi = 0
Choose entering/leaving signs consistently.
ΣΔu = 0
Follow one closed path in one chosen direction. Reversing traversal reverses every term.
U = Us + RI / U = Us − RI
For the source-plus-series-resistor branch: current enters its positive output terminal / leaves it.
symbols: Signed voltage change, terminal voltage and source voltage, volts (V).
examples: Teacher node: I₁ + I₃ = I₂ + I₄ + I₅. Generalised boundary examples: I₁ + I₂ = I₃, or I₁ + I₂ = I₃ = I₄ + I₅.
Teacher rectangle: U₁ − U₂ + U₃ − U₄ = 0. Opposing-source loop: Us₂ + R₂I₂ + R₁I₁ − Us₁ = 0.
traps: KCL and KVL do not require linear elements; superposition does.
An imaginary closing path can include the unknown voltage between two terminals.
Do not change current references merely because you reverse the loop traversal.

branch-analysis.title: Branch-current equation setup
definitions: Assign one reference current to each branch. Write independent node and loop equations, then interpret the signs.
I₁ and I₂ arrive upward in the source branches; I₃ and I₄ flow downward; I₅ flows from top-left node a to top-right node b. Bottom conductor is common.
rules: I₁ − I₃ − I₅ = 0; I₅ + I₂ − I₄ = 0
Two independent KCL equations at nodes a and b.
I₃R₃ + I₁R₁ − Us₁ = 0
Left loop.
I₅R₅ + I₄R₄ − I₃R₃ = 0
Middle loop.
Us₂ − I₂R₂ − I₄R₄ = 0
Right loop.
symbols: Resistances in the corresponding branches, ohms (Ω).
examples: n = 3 and b = 5 → 2 independent KCL + 3 independent loop equations = 5 equations for 5 currents.
The teacher gives symbolic component values here. Setting up this equation system is the intended result; do not invent numerical currents.
traps: The bottom-node equation follows from the other two and adds no independent information.
A negative solution means current flows opposite its assigned arrow. A mesh-current unknown is not automatically a branch-current unknown.

superposition.title: Source-by-source contributions
definitions: In a linear circuit, add the signed voltage/current responses from independent sources acting separately.
Set its prescribed value to zero: ideal voltage source → short; ideal current source → open. Retain resistances.
Stay active if present. The current course examples use independent sources.
rules: I = I₁ + I₂ + …; U = U₁ + U₂ + …
Use the same reference for every contribution. Sources may also be considered in groups.
P = R(I₁ + I₂ + …)²
Calculate power from the final total current; do not add separate-source powers.
symbols: Resistance in ohms; dissipated power in watts.
examples: Course E2: +2 A + (−1 A) = 1 A downward. E3: 3 A + 5 A = 8 A rightward.
Course E4: marked bottom leftward current = 6.2 A. E5: 18 V and 9 V branches contribute 2 A + 1 A = 3 A downward through 4 Ω.
For the first two-source example, calculate and add each branch’s two signed contributions separately. Use the retained teacher diagrams for each circuit.
traps: Superposition is a linear-circuit method. Power is not a linear response.
Suppress only the source being turned off—not its internal resistance or an entire branch.

thevenin.title: Thévenin equivalent at the load port
definitions: The two terminals where the external load attaches. Neither terminal has to be ground.
A voltage source in series with a resistance having the same external terminal relationship.
rules: Uth = Uoc = Va − Vb
Remove only the load and find the open-circuit voltage at its port.
Rth = resistance seen into the port
Suppress independent voltage sources to shorts and independent current sources to opens. Keep resistors.
IL = Uth/(Rth + RL)
Reconnect the load in series with the equivalent resistance.
symbols: Equivalent voltage, open-circuit voltage and node potentials, volts (V).
Equivalent resistance and load resistance, ohms (Ω). The course also labels equivalent resistance R₀.
Current through the reconnected load, amperes (A).
examples: Teacher 8 Ω bridge load: Va = 4 V, Vb = −10 V → Uth = 14 V.
Rth = (2 Ω || 2 Ω) + 5 Ω = 6 Ω. Reconnect RL = 8 Ω → IL = 14/(6+8) = 1 A from a to b.
traps: Remove only the chosen load; preserve the rest of the network and its connections.
Dependent sources stay active. A test source may be needed in problems containing them.

norton.title: Norton equivalent and the same load result
definitions: A current source in parallel with an equivalent resistance.
The current through an ideal short across the selected load port, with the load removed.
rules: IN = Isc; RN = Rth
Find the short-circuit current and the same equivalent resistance as Thévenin.
Rth = Uoc/Isc
Only when this ratio is defined and finite.
IL = IN RN/(RN + RL)
Two parallel branches: RN and the external load RL.
Uth = IN RN
Convert between the finite practical source equivalents.
symbols: Norton, port short-circuit and load currents, amperes (A).
Norton, Thévenin and external load resistances, ohms (Ω).
Port open-circuit and Thévenin voltages, volts (V).
examples: Same teacher bridge: IN = 14/6 A = 7/3 A, in parallel with 6 Ω.
With the 8 Ω load: IL = (7/3) × 6/(6+8) = 1 A. It must agree with the Thévenin result.
traps: The current-source arrow points toward the positive output terminal of its voltage-source equivalent.
In the two-branch current-divider expression, the numerator uses RN, not RL.

transient-intro.title: Switching, stored energy and settling
definitions: The changing interval after a disturbance, as the circuit moves toward a new operating state. Its duration depends on the circuit.
After settling under constant sources, currents and voltages are constant. AC steady state can be periodic.
A change in connections, component values or the supply. A transient occurs when the stored state must change.
rules: Wₑ = ½CuC²; Wₘ = ½LiL²
A capacitor stores electric-field energy; an inductor stores magnetic-field energy. Ordinary finite switching cannot instantly change uC or iL.
iC = C duC/dt; uL = L diL/dt
Changing capacitor voltage requires current; changing inductor current requires voltage, using passive references.
symbols: Capacitance in farads (F); inductance in henries (H).
Voltage across the capacitor (V); current through the inductor (A). C and L label the element.
Electric-field and magnetic-field stored energy, joules (J).
Rate of change with time; t is in seconds.
Source voltage (V), resistance (Ω); resistor–capacitor / resistor–inductor circuits.
examples: Teacher’s lamps: a resistor-branch lamp lights immediately; an inductor-branch lamp brightens gradually; a capacitor-branch lamp flashes then fades as charging current falls.
Initially empty simple RC: uC starts at 0 and approaches Us. Initially empty simple RL: iL starts at 0 and approaches Us/R.
Course applications: RC threshold delay, inductive spark/ignition and fluorescent-lamp starting. Stored energy can produce a large voltage when an inductive current path is interrupted.
traps: A resistor stores no field energy in this ideal model. Its algebraic voltage/current may change immediately.
A switch action with no change required in the stored state can produce no nontrivial transient.
The continuity statements assume ordinary finite excitation, not imposed ideal impulses.

switching.title: Initial conditions and the switching laws
definitions: Immediately before / immediately after the switching event at t = 0. These are two limits at the same event.
Capacitor voltage and inductor current keep their values across an ordinary finite switching event. They may change continuously afterward.
rules: First solve the old circuit. Carry these two stored-state quantities into the new circuit.
DC steady state: iC = 0; uL = 0
Replace an ideal capacitor with an open and an ideal inductor with a short only for a settled DC circuit.
At 0+: C → known voltage constraint; L → known current constraint
Use their initial values and solve the new connections with KCL/KVL. Only a zero initial capacitor voltage permits a momentary short; only zero initial inductor current permits a momentary open.
symbols: Capacitor voltage (V); inductor current (A). C and L are element labels.
Capacitor current (A); inductor voltage (V). These can jump at switching.
Kirchhoff’s current law / Kirchhoff’s voltage law, from Chapter 1.
Direct current; here the settled constant-source condition.
examples: Teacher E1: L becomes a short and C an open in DC steady state. Two 2 Ω branches give 1 Ω; the 6 V supply sees 2 + 1 = 3 Ω, so total current is 2 A. Each conducting branch takes 1 A and uC = 2 V.
Teacher bypass example: before switching, iL = 6/(2k + 2k) = 1.5 mA and uC = 3 V. Immediately afterward those same values remain, even though the node fed directly by the source becomes 6 V.
Teacher initially unenergized network: uC(0+) = 0 and iL(0+) = 0. The capacitor holds its parallel node at 0 V at that instant; the feed current is 6/R and flows into C.
traps: Do not carry every old current or voltage unchanged. Only the storage-state continuity constraints apply.
Do not use C = open and L = short automatically at 0+.
A circuit containing both L and C may need a higher-order full response even though both switching laws still hold.

three-values.title: The three-element method
definitions: One independent storage state, or an equivalent single storage element, with a first-order differential equation.
Initial value f(0+), final value f(∞), and time constant τ. “Elements” here means three quantities, not three physical components.
The final value is the destination. The exponential multiplies the remaining difference from that destination.
rules: Stable linear first-order circuit; fixed post-switch connections and constant sources, t ≥ 0. Restart the analysis for another switching interval.
τRC = Rseen C; τRL = L/Rseen

Look into the storage element’s terminals in the post-switch circuit. Suppress independent voltage sources to shorts and independent current sources to opens. Keep resistances; dependent sources, if present, remain active.
Initial → old circuit; final and τ → new circuit
For initial state use continuity. For final DC values open C and short L with sources active. Suppress sources only when finding Rseen.
At t = τ: 36.8% of the initial-to-final difference remains
63.2% of the change is completed. Your slides use 3τ as about settled (5% remains); 5τ leaves 0.67%. Neither is an exact end.
RC duC/dt + uC = Us; L diL/dt + RiL = Us
KVL plus the element law explains the exponential for simple series RC and RL circuits.
symbols: The chosen voltage (V) or current (A), its starting value, and its final value. ∞ means the long-time limit.
Time constant and elapsed time, both seconds (s).
Equivalent resistance seen by C or L after switching, in ohms (Ω). “seen” names the viewpoint.
Capacitance (F), inductance (H), constant source voltage (V); s labels the source.
e ≈ 2.718, the exponential base. RC = resistor–capacitor; RL = resistor–inductor.
Convert units carefully: 1 F = 10⁶ µF = 10¹² pF.
Series resistance (Ω), capacitor voltage (V), inductor current (A).
examples: Initial-value E4: uC(0+) = 3 V; iL(0+) = 1.5 mA. The bypassed feed makes the new node 6 V: iC(0+) = (6−3)/1k = 3 mA; source current = 4.5 mA; uL(0+) = 6−(1.5 mA×2k) = 3 V.

Other initial-value examples: the settled 6 V/2 kΩ inductor retains 3 mA; the initially empty 10 V LC network has iL(0+) = 0 and iC(0+) = 0; the 1 A-source example retains iL = 1 A, so the newly connected resistor initially carries 0 A.

Teacher 20 V/1 kΩ/1 H example: initially empty L has iL(0+) = 0 and uL(0+) = 20 V. After a long time iL = 20 mA. Rerouting that current through a 500 kΩ meter gives a 10 kV magnitude; with the marked downward voltage reference, the reading is −10 kV.
Final-value examples: the 4 mA source splits into equal branches, giving iL(∞) = 2 mA. The capacitor divider gives uC(∞) = 10×3/(4||4+3) = 6 V, with resistor values in kΩ.
Time constants: L = 1 H sees 3+3 = 6 Ω, so τ = 1/6 s. The capacitor sees 6k||6k||3k = 1.5 kΩ, so τ = 1500 C seconds. The slide’s “1.5 Ω” label misses k.
Bridge review: 18 V dividers 3k/6k and 6k/3k give midpoint voltages 12 V and 6 V. Thus uC(∞) = 6 V, left positive; Rseen = (3k||6k)+(6k||3k) = 4 kΩ; τ = 4000 C seconds.
traps: Check t = 0 and t → ∞ in your equation: they must reproduce the two values you found.
Two independent storage states generally cannot be represented by one exponential.
For positive Rseen, increasing R slows RC but speeds RL; use the correct time-constant formula.
The 10 kV meter result is an ideal model calculation; the practical transient applications in the slides include ignition, flash lamps, spot welding and wire-explosion spraying.

rc-response.title: RC charging, discharging and complete response
definitions: No initial stored energy; an applied source builds the response.
No applied source after switching; initial stored energy drives the response.
Initial stored energy and the post-switch source both contribute.
rules: τ = Rseen C; uC(t) = Uf + (U0 − Uf)e^(−t/τ)
General first-order RC voltage under constant post-switch excitation. For a simple source–R–C loop, Rseen = R and Uf = Us.
Uncharged → Us: uC = Us(1 − e^(−t/RC)); iC = (Us/R)e^(−t/RC)
Simple series RC charge: uC starts at 0; iC starts at Us/R and tends to 0.
Discharge through R: uC = U0e^(−t/RC); iC = −(U0/R)e^(−t/RC)
Current reference enters C’s positive terminal. Negative means the actual discharge current leaves that terminal.
Us1 → Us2: uC = Us2 + (Us1 − Us2)e^(−t/RC)
Initially settled at Us1, then connected through R to Us2. iC = [(Us2−Us1)/R]e^(−t/RC).
t = −τ ln[(Utarget − Uf)/(U0 − Uf)]
Target lies strictly between unequal initial and final values. The logarithm’s ratio must be between 0 and 1.
symbols: Capacitor voltage in volts; capacitor current in amperes. C labels the capacitor.
Source voltage, old source voltage and new source voltage (V).
Initial, final and requested capacitor voltages (V); f means final.
Resistance and equivalent seen resistance (Ω), capacitance (F), time constant (s).
Natural logarithm and its base e ≈ 2.718.
examples: Video calculation: R = 1 kΩ, C = 500 µF, Us = 20 V → τ = 0.5 s. To reach 18 V: t = −0.5 ln(0.1) ≈ 1.151 s, or 2.303τ.
Complete-response illustration of the teacher’s formula: U0 = 10 V, Uf = 4 V → uC(t) = 4+6e^(−t/τ). With current into C’s positive terminal, iC is negative as the voltage falls.
Teacher complete-response table has reused zero-state entries. Use uC(0+) = Us1 and iC(0+) = (Us2−Us1)/R, consistent with its main equation.
traps: The charging formula that starts at zero is not valid for every initially charged capacitor.
For a general network, the final voltage is its DC port voltage, not automatically the supply voltage.
An exponential approaches its endpoint asymptotically; “fully charged after 5τ” is an approximation.

rl-response.title: RL response and the teacher’s decay example
definitions: Inductor current cannot jump at ordinary finite switching. Its voltage can change immediately to maintain that initial current.
After switching, trace the actual closed path available to the stored inductor current. The old supply resistance is not automatically the new Rseen.
rules: iL(t) = If + (I0 − If)e^(−t/τ); τ = L/Rseen
Stable linear first-order RL circuit with constant post-switch excitation.
Zero-state buildup: iL = (Us/R)(1−e^(−tR/L))
Initially empty series RL connected to Us through R.
Source-free decay: iL = I0e^(−t/τ); uL = −Rseen I0e^(−t/τ)
A resistive decay path remains. For passive references uL = L diL/dt: falling positive current gives negative uL.
WL = ½LiL²; pL = uL iL
During decay, pL is negative under passive references: stored magnetic energy returns to the resistors.
symbols: Initial, final and instantaneous inductor currents (A); L labels the inductor.
Passive terminal voltage; induced source EMF, both volts. Their references are opposite: uL = −eL.
Inductance (H), resistance seen after switching (Ω), time constant (s).
Stored magnetic energy (J); instantaneous absorbed inductor power (W).
Constant source voltage (V), series resistance (Ω); RL means resistor–inductor.
examples: Teacher initial circuit: 3 A divides between a 2 Ω branch and a (1 Ω + ideal shorted L) branch. iL(0−) = 3×2/(2+1) = 2 A. The feed resistor does not change that current division.
After the switch moves, Rseen = 1+(2||2) = 2 Ω. L = 1 H → τ = 1/2 = 0.5 s; If = 0.
Substitute the three values: iL(t) = 2e^(−2t) A. Differentiate: uL(t) = −4e^(−2t) V with the marked downward passive voltage reference.
At t = 0+: iL = 2 A and uL = −4 V. At 0.5 s: iL ≈ 0.736 A and uL ≈ −1.472 V. Both tend to zero. The current direction stays the same while energy is released.
traps: An ideal inductor is a DC steady-state short, not a short throughout the transient.
Do not set current to zero just because the original source was disconnected.
An open inductor with no modeled discharge path cannot be treated as an ordinary finite-resistance exponential.

ac-waveforms.title: Sinusoidal AC: size, speed and phase
definitions: Alternating current reverses direction; alternating voltage reverses polarity. DC means direct current. A positive-only pulse train is unidirectional pulsating DC in this course.
Peak is the largest magnitude. RMS means root mean square: the equivalent resistor-heating value. It is not the signed average.
The angle in the sine function. Initial phase is that angle at t = 0; larger phase leads for same-frequency signals using one sine/cosine convention.
rules: i(t) = Im sin(ωt + ψ); T = 1/f; ω = 2πf
Use consistent angle units. Frequency f is cycles per second; ω is radians per second.
Pure sinusoids only. The course uses uppercase I, U, E for RMS; lowercase i, u, e for instantaneous values.
φ = ψu − ψi
Same-frequency signals expressed with the same reference: positive φ → voltage leads/current lags; negative φ → voltage lags/current leads.
Resistor average power: P = U²/R = I²R
Use RMS voltage/current. A sine’s full-cycle signed average is zero, but its heating is not.
symbols: Peak current (A), voltage and source EMF (V); m means maximum.
RMS current (A), voltage and source EMF (V). RMS = root mean square.
Initial phase, voltage/current initial phases, voltage-minus-current phase difference; degrees or radians consistently.
examples: Teacher: f = 2 Hz → T = 0.5 s and ω = 4π rad/s.
i = 10 sin(1000t+30°) A: Im = 10 A, I ≈ 7.07 A, initial phase +30°. Convert the degree offset to radians when evaluating alongside ωt.
Teacher: u = 311 sin(314t−60°) V and i = 100 sin(314t+30°) A → φ = −90°: current leads voltage by 90°.
Constant-resistance 300 V-rated heater at 220 V RMS: power ratio = (220/300)² ≈ 0.538. The 220 V and 380 V supply ratings in the slides are RMS.
The rotating-coil alternator reverses induced polarity as it rotates. The slides ask about 50/60 Hz, ballast frequency and high-frequency advantages, but supply no specific ballast frequency answer.
traps: A changing magnitude alone does not establish AC in the course’s classification.
60 Hz means 60 complete cycles per second, with two direction reversals per cycle.
The video’s P = UI and peak-power shortcut apply to its in-phase sinusoidal examples, not every AC load.

phasors.title: Phasors and complex arithmetic
definitions: A complex number recording a sinusoid’s magnitude and initial phase. Frequency is shared problem information, not supplied by the phasor alone.
An anticlockwise rotating vector’s vertical projection gives a sine wave. Relative angles stay fixed for signals of the same frequency.
rules: a+jb = M(cosψ+j sinψ) = Me^(jψ) = M∠ψ
Rectangular, trigonometric, exponential and polar forms of the same number. j² = −1.
M = √(a²+b²); ψ = atan2(b,a); a = M cosψ; b = M sinψ
Keep the correct quadrant; ordinary arctan(b/a) alone can give the wrong direction.
Add/subtract in rectangular form; multiply/divide in polar form
Add corresponding components. For multiplication multiply magnitudes/add angles; for division divide magnitudes/subtract angles.
i(t) = √2 I sin(ωt+ψ) ↔ Ĩ = I∠ψ
Course sine reference and RMS phasor. A peak phasor uses Im = √2 I instead.
×j → +90° rotation; ×(−j) → −90° rotation
Neither rotation changes magnitude.
symbols: Imaginary unit, real component, imaginary component and nonnegative magnitude. Components have the same units as the phasor.
Current phasor (A); voltage phasor (V). The accent distinguishes a phasor from a scalar RMS magnitude.
RMS current (A), shared angular frequency (rad/s), time (s).
examples: (1+j)/(√3/2+j/2) = √2∠15°. Multiplying that result by (1/2+j√3/2) gives √2∠75°.
Therefore i(t) ≈ 16.8√2 sin(314t−10.9°) A. The RMS result is 16.8 A; do not add 12.7+11 as magnitudes.
Ĩ = 20∠30° A needs a separately given ω to become a waveform: i(t)=20√2 sin(ωt+30°) A. It does not itself imply ω = 1000 rad/s.
traps: Do not add phase angles when adding phasors.
Do not mix peak and RMS phasors in the same calculation.
Do not add different-frequency signals as one fixed-frequency phasor.

impedance.title: Pure resistance, inductance and capacitance
definitions: Complex ratio of voltage phasor to current phasor. Magnitude sets the voltage/current size ratio; angle sets their phase difference.
Here both are positive magnitudes. Their impedance signs differ: +j for an inductor; −j for a capacitor.
rules: ZR = R; Ũ = RĨ; U = RI
Ideal resistor with passive references: voltage and current in phase.
XL = ωL = 2πfL; ZL = jXL; Ũ = jXLĨ
Ideal inductor: voltage leads current by 90°. Magnitudes obey U = XL I. XL increases with frequency.
XC = 1/(ωC); ZC = −jXC = 1/(jωC); Ũ = −jXCĨ
Ideal capacitor: current leads voltage by 90°. Magnitudes obey U = XC I. XC decreases with frequency.
iL = Im sinωt → uL = ωLIm cosωt
A derivative of sine is cosine: the inductor voltage is 90° ahead. Similarly uC = Um sinωt gives iC = ωCUm cosωt.
symbols: Resistance, inductive/capacitive reactance magnitudes, complex impedance, all ohms (Ω).
RMS voltage/current magnitudes and their corresponding phasors, V/A.
Identify the resistor / inductor / capacitor. j means a +90° rotation.
Peak current (A), peak voltage (V), time (s); m means maximum.
examples: If I = 2 A and R = 5 Ω, U = 10 V in phase. If XL = 5 Ω, U = 10 V with voltage 90° ahead. If XC = 5 Ω, U = 10 V with voltage 90° behind current.
Teacher capacitor slide: the repeated phrase “voltage leads” and symbol XL are typos there. Use current leading voltage and Ũ = −jXCĨ.
traps: Do not treat a reactance magnitude as a real resistance: you would lose the phase.
The simple laws describe ideal elements in sinusoidal steady state, with consistent reference polarities.

series-rlc.title: Series RLC and series impedances
definitions: All elements carry the same current. Voltage phasors add by KVL; their magnitudes usually do not.
Horizontal side R, signed vertical side X, hypotenuse |Z|. Its angle φ is voltage phase minus current phase.
rules: Z = R+j(XL−XC) = R+jX; Ũ = ZĨ
Same-frequency sinusoidal steady state, with passive element references.
|Z| = √(R²+X²); φ = atan2(X,R); Ĩ = Ũ/Z
Scalar RMS magnitudes obey U = |Z|I. For positive R, arctan(X/R) gives the same principal angle.
X > 0 → inductive; X < 0 → capacitive; X = 0 → resistive at the terminals
Current lags voltage / leads voltage / is in phase, respectively.
Complex series voltage divider; use the full impedances, not their magnitudes.
Special cases: R; jXL; −jXC; R+jXL; R−jXC; j(XL−XC)
R, L, C, RL, RC and LC, respectively. Omit the absent elements.
symbols: Complex impedance, its magnitude, resistance and signed net reactance (Ω).
Positive inductive/capacitive reactance magnitudes (Ω); impedance/voltage-minus-current angle.
Supply voltage phasor (V), common current phasor (A), section voltage phasors (V).
Section impedances (Ω); “total” means the complete series combination.
RMS voltage (V) and current (A); RLC means resistor–inductor–capacitor.
examples: Teacher opening question: UR = UL = UC = 1 V. With current at 0°, Ũ = 1+j−j = 1 V, not 3 V.
Teacher divider: Ũs=10∠0° V, Z1=3+j2 Ω and Z2=2+j3 Ω. Ztotal=5+j5 Ω, Ĩ=1−j1 A. Ũ1=5−j1 V and Ũ2=5+j1 V; their sum is 10 V.
traps: U = ZI is not a scalar-magnitude formula when Z is complex; write U = |Z|I.
Large individual inductor/capacitor voltages can cancel in the phasor sum.
The video’s resonance frequency formula is optional enrichment here; learn the teacher’s requested impedance and divider calculations first.

parallel-rlc.title: Parallel RLC and parallel impedances
definitions: All branches share the same voltage. KCL adds their current phasors.
Inductor and capacitor currents can cancel at the supply while each branch still carries current and exchanges stored energy.
rules: Ĩ = ĨR+ĨL+ĨC; with Ũ at 0°: Ĩ = U/R − jU/XL + jU/XC
Pure R/L/C branches: resistor current is in phase, inductor current at −90°, capacitor current at +90°.
Two parallel complex impedances, when the denominators are defined.
Current divider: use the opposite branch’s impedance in the numerator.
Ĩk = Ũ/Zk; Ĩ = ΣĨk
Alternative method: solve each branch then add in rectangular form.
symbols: Total, resistor, inductor and capacitor current phasors (A).
Common voltage phasor (V), branch and equivalent impedances (Ω); eq = equivalent.
Branch label; sum of all branch contributions.
Current phasors in branches 1 and 2 (A); s labels the supply; RLC means resistor–inductor–capacitor.
examples: Teacher’s equal 5 A cases: R+L+C → 5−j5+j5 = 5 A. L+C alone → −j5+j5 = 0 A at the supply. R+C → 5+j5 = 5√2∠45° A.
Teacher E1: Ĩs=5∠0° A, Z1=2+j2 Ω, Z2=3+j3 Ω → Ĩ1=3 A, Ĩ2=2 A, Zeq=1.2+j1.2 Ω and Ũ=6+j6 V.
Check E2 independently: Zeq≈194.682−j163.188 Ω. 220/Zeq gives the same total current. The slides’ 0.862∠39.6° result uses earlier rounding.
traps: Do not add current magnitudes. Add real and imaginary components.
Use full complex Z values in the divider.
Zero total reactive supply current does not imply zero current in the reactive branches.

average-power.title: Instantaneous and average power
definitions: p(t) = u(t)i(t), with current entering the marked + terminal. Positive means energy enters the element; negative means it returns energy.
The mean of p(t) over a complete cycle, measured in watts. Ideal L and C return their stored energy over a full cycle, so their average real power is zero.
rules: P = (1/T)∫₀ᵀp(t)dt = UI cosφ
Sinusoidal steady state; U and I are RMS magnitudes; φ = ψu−ψi.
Pure R: p(t) = UI[1−cos(2ωt)]; P = UI = I²R = U²/R
Using in-phase sine waveforms. p never becomes negative; it varies at twice the electrical frequency.
Pure L: P = 0; pure C: P = 0
Their instantaneous absorbed power alternates between positive storage and negative return. Zero average does not mean zero instantaneous power.
symbols: Voltage-minus-current phase difference; individual initial phases.
Resistance (Ω); integrate over one full period to obtain energy, then divide by T for average power.
examples: Teacher correction: the resistor’s identity is 1−cos(2ωt), not 1−cos²(ωt). The pure-inductor slide repeats resistor formulas by mistake; its correct average real power is zero.
For L with i=√2 I sinωt, u=√2 U cosωt, so p=UI sin(2ωt). For C with u=√2 U sinωt, i=√2 I cosωt, the displayed p has the same algebraic form because the chosen time reference differs.
If U=100 V, I=5 A and current lags voltage by 60°, P=100×5×cos60°=250 W. The product UI is 500 VA, not 500 W.
traps: Use RMS values in P=UI cosφ; peak magnitudes need a factor of ½.
Compare instantaneous-power plots using the same voltage/current phase reference.
An ideal capacitor or inductor can have zero average real power while exchanging substantial energy.

power-triangle.title: Reactive power, apparent power and power factor
definitions: Signed measure of sinusoidal energy exchange: positive for passive inductive loads, negative for passive capacitive loads. Units: var.
RMS voltage × RMS current, in volt-amperes (VA). It combines real power and reactive exchange; it is not their arithmetic sum.
P/S = cosφ for sinusoidal voltage/current. State leading or lagging as well as the number. It is not an energy-efficiency percentage.
rules: P = UI cosφ; Q = UI sinφ; S = UI = √(P²+Q²)
Sinusoidal steady state; consistent passive references and RMS magnitudes.
Pure R: Q=0; pure L: Q=+UI; pure C: Q=−UI
For L, Q=I²XL=U²/XL. For C, |Q|=I²XC=U²/XC; retain the negative sign when adding.
Ptotal = ΣPk; Qtotal = ΣQk; Stotal = √(Ptotal²+Qtotal²)
Add signed real/reactive powers first. Apparent-power magnitudes generally do not add.
PF = P/S; tanφ = Q/P
Power triangle: P horizontal, signed Q vertical, S hypotenuse. Use ratios only when their denominators are nonzero.
With voltage at 0°: Ĩ = I cosφ − jI sinφ
In-phase current component IP=I cosφ gives P=U IP. Inductive current has a negative imaginary component.
symbols: Active power (W/kW), signed reactive power (var/kvar), apparent power (VA/kVA).
Power factor (no unit); voltage phase minus current phase. Positive φ is lagging current; negative φ is leading current.
Active current component and RMS total current (A); RMS voltage (V).
Positive reactance magnitudes (Ω); sum; branch/component label.
examples: Worked illustration of the course addition rule: 300 W resistor plus +400 var inductor → S=√(300²+400²)=500 VA, PF=0.6 lagging. Apparent power is not 700 VA.
Add a capacitor with Q=−400 var: net Q=0, P remains 300 W and S becomes 300 VA in the ideal model.
Teacher’s capacitor Q is printed as a positive magnitude. Use negative capacitor Q when combining it with inductive Q.
traps: Reactive power is not the heat loss I²R. Ideal reactive elements exchange energy rather than dissipating average real power.
A cosine alone cannot distinguish leading from lagging.
The reviewed slides do not teach a separate capacitor-sizing procedure; do not treat it as required here.
